org.portico.impl.hla1516e.types

Class HLA1516eHandle

  • java.lang.Object
    • org.portico.impl.hla1516e.types.HLA1516eHandle
  • All Implemented Interfaces:
    hla.rti1516e.AttributeHandle, hla.rti1516e.DimensionHandle, hla.rti1516e.FederateHandle, hla.rti1516e.InteractionClassHandle, hla.rti1516e.MessageRetractionHandle, hla.rti1516e.ObjectClassHandle, hla.rti1516e.ObjectInstanceHandle, hla.rti1516e.ParameterHandle, hla.rti1516e.RegionHandle, hla.rti1516e.TransportationTypeHandle, Serializable

    public class HLA1516eHandle
extends Object
implements hla.rti1516e.AttributeHandle, hla.rti1516e.DimensionHandle, hla.rti1516e.FederateHandle, hla.rti1516e.InteractionClassHandle, hla.rti1516e.MessageRetractionHandle, hla.rti1516e.ObjectClassHandle, hla.rti1516e.ObjectInstanceHandle, hla.rti1516e.ParameterHandle, hla.rti1516e.RegionHandle, hla.rti1516e.TransportationTypeHandle
    Generic handle class. All the IEEE 1516e handle types provide the same interface. Rather than signal that there should be just a single handle type, the specification defines a bunch of independent interfaces (all the same, mercifully). As such, we just provide a single implementation.

    Technically believe this may not be fully specification compliant, in that you could call equals(Object) on a handle of two separate types, and get true if the underyling values are the same, such as in the following example: 

     AttributeHandle ahandle = ...(1);
 FederateHandle fhandle = ....(1);
 assert ahandle.equals(fhandle); // would work, but should it...?
    Ultimately, I don't care. So there.
